1:
Keil and Delitzsch set the chapter against what precedes. The previous word had figured Israel as a wild and useless vine; but since God had planted that vine himself, the rebellious nation could still plead its election and argue that he would not reject a people taken into covenant. This chapter removes that confidence by showing Israel no better by nature than the nations around it, and sunk lower through ingratitude. They mark the turn at the end too, since the Lord remains mindful of his covenant and will restore Jerusalem alongside Sodom and Samaria, though to the deep shame of Israel.

Henry begins with the geography of the two ministries. The prophet was among the captives in Babylon and wrote for Jerusalem, while another prophet resident at Jerusalem wrote for the captives, and neither took the other help as any affront. Each sent what the other audience needed, consolation for men in exile and conviction for men in the city. Gill adds that the commission could be discharged by writing, the prophet being in Chaldea with the exiles.

On the command to make the city know her abominations Henry hangs five observations. Sins are not merely provocations God is angry at but abominations he hates as contrary to his nature, and the sins of this city especially, since profaneness looks most odious in those who profess religion. Though the place was one of great knowledge it was loath to know its own abominations, men being so partial in their own favour that they can hardly be made to own their badness, but deny it or palliate it. We need to know our sins in order to confess them and to justify God in what he brings on us. And it is the work of ministers to set the glass of the law before sinners and tell them plainly of their faults.

Calvin makes the same point and traces it further down. Men are often so blinded by their vices that they cannot perceive what is plain to everyone else, and this people was drunk with pride and had blinded itself by its own flatteries. We think such admonitions superfluous, he says, until God drags us into the light and sets our sins before our eyes. No one lacks a conscience that reproves him, since the law is written on all hearts; but that self-knowledge is cold and wrapped in darkness, so a man partly conscious of his fault grows willingly hardened while he indulges himself. What makes the case worse is that the people took pleasure in the superstitions condemned, since the foulest idolatry is easily disguised under the pretext that God is worshipped by it.

Clarke frames the chapter as a manifesto and does not soften his estimate. Mercy is set out under the figure of a person taking up an exposed infant and afterwards marrying her; ingratitude under a wife proving false to an indulgent husband; and restoration after correction at the close. He judges the state of the nation before the captivity the most profligate of all the nations of the earth, and warns against reading the whole as figure, since not everything here is metaphorical: where there was so much idolatry there must have been the vices that go with it. He names the sixth satire of Juvenal as the nearest counterpart he knows, and says general remarks are all a commentator is justified in bestowing on so caustic an invective.

Calvin notes that Scripture does not always date the origin of this people alike. Sometimes it goes back to Abraham before God drew him, when he worshipped idols; sometimes it begins at the covenant by which he and his posterity were chosen. Here the reckoning starts where a small band multiplied into a nation despite oppression. Gill notes that the city stands for the whole people, whose idolatries were committed openly and never confessed.
3:
Calvin puts the obvious objection first. If God adopted Abraham two centuries before, why is that covenant left out of account here? His answer is that the sentence describes only what they were in themselves. God never departed from his purpose, but the people had corrupted themselves in Egypt; another prophet says as much when he calls them born of a harlot, which is not an accusation against actual women but a way of saying they were unworthy to be reckoned the seed of Abraham. Though God stood firm in his covenant, they had by faithlessness cut themselves off, so that the promise was extinct on their side and their adoption dead and buried. One translator, he notes, renders the word root, where he prefers nativity.

Ellicott argues from the grammar that the reference is spiritual rather than natural, the nouns being plural in the original, and compares men addressed as sons of the devil and as rulers of Sodom. The two tribes named are frequently put for the whole of Canaan, and the dealings of the patriarchs were particularly with the second; he adds that this once powerful nation had almost faded from history but that its monuments were just beginning to be deciphered.

Clarke takes the insult at full strength: it would dishonour Abraham to say they sprang from him, and as the Canaanites were accursed so are they. He compares the preacher who called the Pharisees a brood of vipers, then reaches for a pagan parallel, the reproach thrown at Aeneas that he was not born of a goddess but hewn out of a rock and suckled by tigers. That is strong, he says, but the prophet exceeds it far.

When the birth falls is disputed. Gill offers the call out of Ur or, as he prefers, the time in Egypt when the people multiplied and came out as a nation. Wesley takes it of the day Abraham was called from his idolatry. Ellicott places it at the passage from the patriarchs family to a nation in bondage, and observes that no other people ever became a nation so despised and enslaved, so that humanly speaking national life was an impossibility.

The birth is described in unusual technical detail. Keil and Delitzsch explain that cutting the navel-string frees the child from the blood that fed it in the womb, and that if the cutting and tying are neglected the child must perish once the placenta decomposes. They also refuse one proposed derivation of a word here, neither sense of that root fitting. Clarke supplies the procedure, the cord knotted so the sides unite, the child washed and sometimes salted to firm the skin, and finally swathed to hold the muscles until they can carry the body. On that last step he has an opinion of his own: among savage peoples it is neglected, and the less of it the better, since such compression impedes the circulation and the lungs.

Ellicott thinks neither text nor margin catches the word rendered to supple, and proposes to cleanse; rubbing a newborn with salt is still found in the east and is recommended by Galen, while tight swaddling is common even in Italy. Calvin gives the same account of the salt, which hardens the flesh, though care must be taken not to harden it too much. He anchors the figure in history: the people were driven to servile labour and their male children ordered killed, so that they were in a manner buried in Egypt. Clarke adds that the exposure in the field alludes to nations who left out to the beasts any child deformed or unwanted. Gill takes the unpitied state as the condition of the people under their taskmasters; Wesley makes it besides an apt illustration of the natural state of all the children of men, their father too having worshipped strange gods before he was called.
6:
Ellicott makes a syntactical point that changes the sense of the first verse. The original contains neither the word when nor the words supplied in italics, and the phrase about the blood belongs with the speaking rather than the command, so that the word live was spoken while the child lay unclean. He notes that the Chaldee paraphrast took the other connection and drew from it a double reading, of the blood of circumcision and the blood of the passover; and he prefers the marginal trodden under foot to polluted. On the later verse he distinguishes two visits, one in infancy under bondage and one when the child had become a nation, as Wesley also does.

Gill takes the passing by as a traveller noticing an exposed infant, or the daughter of Pharaoh at the river. Calvin keeps the traveller, who casts his eyes to either side and attends to anything unusual, and reads the doubled I have seen elsewhere as meaning God watched them continually while seeming to shut his eyes. He makes the command their whole preservation. The word live was not spoken aloud for them to hear but announces what God had determined; and though the phrase about the blood might be read contemptuously, as if he grudged moving a hand where none of us willingly touches putrid gore, the context shows it expresses the secret power by which they were kept alive against nature. A hundred deaths surrounded them, and only that hidden voice sustained them. Wesley says the command sends forth a power to effect what it commands, and Henry that those shall live to whom God commands life.

Henry sets out five things done for the nation: God saved them from the ruin they stood on the brink of; looked on them with an affection that cannot be accounted for, since there was nothing lovely in them, which Henry calls distinguishing love; took them under protection, spreading a skirt as a man did over a woman at the threshing floor; cleared away the reproach their bondage had laid on them; and multiplied them, which Henry notes happened while they were still bondslaves. Clarke describes the child as at once an object of horror and of compassion.

Calvin observes that an exposed infant which keeps its life is still a weak abortion, so the favour is magnified by the people increasing as though nothing had been neglected, seventy-five entering Egypt and hundreds of thousands leaving within two and a half centuries. He excuses the bluntness of the description, the prophet expressing grossly what might have been said more concisely because of the rudeness of the people. Ellicott adjusts the tenses and treats the difficult phrase for ornament as meaning simply beauty; the closing clause, he warns, does not contrast this state with the earlier infancy, but says that while the child grew into full beauty she was still naked and bare.

At the covenant Keil and Delitzsch describe the Lord going past a second time and choosing for his bride a virgin grown to womanhood, the marriage contracted at Sinai; they gloss the spread skirt as the lappet of a garment that served also as a counterpane. Clarke says the same in legal terms, the spread skirt being an initiatory marriage ceremony. Calvin is uneasy with the figure and says why. God here personates a man struck by the beauty of a girl and offering her marriage, but he is not affected as men are, and it is not according to his nature to love as young men do; the accommodation was made because the people could not otherwise be taught. He adds that they had never been lovely until God embraced them, so the love rested on his good pleasure. Wesley draws the double consequence, that those taken into covenant become his subjects, which is their duty, and his treasure, which is their privilege.
9:
Calvin refuses to read the ornaments allegorically. Those who do, he says, fruitlessly conjecture trifles which contradict one another, and their guesses are refuted by the words themselves; he would have readers content with the plain sense, that God poured out all his blessings in enriching this people. Gill takes the opposite course and follows the Targum, which reads the ornaments of the words of the law, adding either good works or, as he prefers, the graces of the Spirit. Clarke reports the same Targum reading, of the tabernacle service, the book of the law and the priestly vestments.

He does give a substantial answer to how the people were adorned. First God embraced them with his favour and promised to be their God, which was their chief honour. Second he cared for them in the desert, appearing by day in a cloud and by night in a pillar of fire, bringing water from the rock, giving daily food as if he had placed it in their mouths, and blessing the land so that its promise of milk and honey proved no empty word.

Calvin notes that a party-coloured garment was the eastern custom, worn by a boy in a shepherd family without pretension to splendour; and asks whether women may adorn themselves so, answering that the prophet does not approve what he relates but uses a common image. He turns the passage on his readers: reflecting on our origin, we are all born children of wrath and, in our spiritual state, like newborn infants lying in our own filth, the image of God not merely defiled by original sin but all but extinct.

Clarke identifies the skin as the kind used to cover the tabernacle; Ellicott calls it a fine leather from some sea creature, the critics differing whether dolphin or dugong; Wesley says eastern peoples had an art of dressing such skins and made their best shoes of them. On the word rendered silk Ellicott notes that it occurs only here and once again, that its meaning is much questioned, and that the translators followed rabbinical tradition; Clarke thinks it the produce of the silkworm, and remarks that he has seen linen of this kind wrapping the finest mummies. On the jewel the three converge. Gill makes it a nose jewel reckoned a great ornament in the east, and cites travellers who report women in Persia and the Levant piercing the nostril for it. Clarke renders the phrase literally as upon the nose and observes that European translators, not knowing what to make of a ring there, moved it to the forehead. Ellicott renders it a nose-ring and says the custom of the time sanctioned it.

Clarke then supplies what he calls the key to the whole chapter, advising the reader to forget the figures and look at the facts. The infant is the low estate of the nation at its origin; the growth to womanhood its increase; the ornaments its ordinances; the marriage the covenant; the harlotry the apostasy into idolatrous worship; the whoredoms with particular nations the sinful alliances made with them; and the lovers brought to strip her the delivery of the people into those same hands. He follows it with an apology for the language, saying that what looks exceptionable now was conformable to that time and would have raised no improper thought in a hearer, since custom sanctions the mode and prevents the abuse; had the prophet spoken in terms we call chaste, he would have lost half his force. Ellicott adds a theological caution. However natural a fruit of neglected grace this sin was, it was still extraordinary, and the people are not called worse than others by mere hyperbole; grace which does not elevate, he says, always reacts by directing to a lower depth.
14:
Calvin will not date the renown narrowly. The phrase covers a continued series of favours running until the people reached their highest happiness, which he places under David. They had not earned their fame by their own virtue nor were noble by native excellence, but by an ornament bestowed; and its reach matters, since they were admired not merely at home but among foreigners. Wesley locates the beauty in their holiness as a people devoted to God, adding that God must have all the glory of it. Gill turns the clause to the beauty of the Church, placed in an imputed righteousness rather than anything of its own.

The turn to the charge is where Calvin is strongest. Nothing is more unworthy, he says, than to grow proud on the pretext of the gifts of God; he takes beauty as his first instance, observing that though it is a gift of God most women who have it are made proud by it, and then extends the fault to everyone. Whatever a man excels in he arrogates more to himself than he ought: riches turn to luxury and pomp, and ability turns acuteness into cunning. Almost all men, he concludes, profane the gifts of God so. The fountain of it he names as immodesty, since once that restraint is thrown off there is no moderation before God or man; the gifts were meant as invitations to gratitude and were turned into material for pride. Clarke says the same in a sentence, that they trusted in riches and alliances without considering where these came from.

Ellicott explains the collapse historically and calls it one of the most striking instances of providence at work in history. The kingdom was raised as a theocracy to great power and wealth, and then trusted in its own beauty. The policy of its greatest king was to make it a powerful empire, losing sight of its character as the kingdom of God, so that the very means taken to aggrandise it became the instruments of its fall. A vast harem gathered from surrounding nations brought idolatry into the palace, while the magnificence was sustained by taxation that supplied the pretext for revolt. When the division came at his death, the empire outside the borders fell apart like a rope of sand, and inside were two petty kingdoms often at war, each inviting stronger neighbours to whose rapacity the whole at last fell prey.

That position, Ellicott adds, put the nation at the mercy of every stronger power and gave impetus to whatever idolatry its masters encouraged; and this is why the figure is not merely harlotry but indiscriminate harlotry, the people never holding to one false god but worshipping the abominations of every nation that prevailed over them. Henry supplies the same history from the other end, dating the idolatry from the latter part of that reign, remarking that he does not remember reading of it earlier, and that it was thereafter the crying sin of the nation until the captivity, checked by reforming kings but never suppressed. Two things were involved, the worship of the true God by images and the worship of false gods outright.

Henry gives four reasons why this sin is figured as whoredom. It violates a marriage covenant, forsaking one husband for a stranger and giving rivals the affection due to him alone. It corrupts the mind and enslaves the spiritual part of a man, subjecting it to sense. It debauches the conscience, so that those who dishonour the divine nature are justly given over to a mind that dishonours their own; and it is a besotting sin, out of whose snare men seldom recover. And it is shameful for those joined to the Lord to join themselves to an idol. Behind it all he sets the cause the text names, that they grew proud on being admired by their neighbours.
16:
Calvin reads the decorated high places as a deliberate advertisement. He compares them to tents pitched where they will be seen, as a woman seeking a crowd might set her standard on a height; a modest woman would have kept to the retirement of an honest matron, whereas these were made conspicuous like a house that hangs out a sign to show itself open to all. Ellicott notes that coloured tapestry adorned places of worship universally in antiquity and was a feature of the tabernacle itself, so that what is censured is the perversion of a thing meant for the glory of God. He renders the last clause as apposition, things which should not come and that which should not take place. Calvin records two other readings, that no instance like this had ever been seen, or that the number of the high places outdid anything the nations had raised; the second he thinks to the purpose.

What the images of men were is the sharpest dispute in the passage, and the commentators take opposite sides by name. Clarke identifies them with the emblems carried in the processions of several ancient cults, comparing the corresponding object in eastern worship and citing the account in Herodotus of such figures borne through the villages. Wesley allows the same possibility more cautiously. Keil and Delitzsch reject it outright. They record the suggestion of Ewald that household gods are meant, hung with ornaments and honoured with spread tables, and deny any such allusion; and say there is still less ground for the fertility reading proposed by Vatke and Movers, of which it is impossible to find the slightest trace among the Israelites, the arguments for it having already been shown by Hitzig to have no force. The context, they conclude, points to no particular kind of idol but to the many varieties of the local worship.

Calvin is interested less in the identification than in what making them implies. The text does not say they simply took gold and silver, and he reads the phrase for the manufactured gods as marking the excess of the appetite, since it is having to do with shadows, as a woman may feed a passion on nothing more than the picture of her paramour. The charge is double, not idolatry only but ingratitude, since they turned to the dishonour of God the very gifts he had bestowed.

Calvin keeps the domestic figure through the offerings. As an immodest woman bestows on others what she received from her husband, so this people wasted on idols what had been given them. On the oil and incense he adds a historical note: the fathers used oil in sacrifice and incense was prescribed in the law, while the nations used both promiscuously and without judgment, so the complaint is that his own herbs were burnt and his own oil poured out for another. The fine flour stands for the best of everything, so a people overflowing with luxuries consumed them badly; and since none of it could be credited to their own industry, the mockery was past bearing.

Gill asks whether the gold and silver were the temple furniture, as an earlier commentator thought, or the household plate providence had given them, which he prefers. Clarke reaches the same conclusion about the vestments, that what belonged to the Lord was used to honour idols. Wesley reads the covering as clothing the images and the oil as burnt in lamps before them, the sweet savour being an attempt to gain the idol favour. Ellicott draws the principle that outlasts the occasion: the heart of the charge is that these gifts came from God and were given away to another, and that charge, he says, must for ever remain true of the perversion of any talent God has given to a use other than his own service.
20:
Ellicott traces a development in the practice charged here. At first it was a ceremony of passing children through fire to consecrate them, and only afterwards an actual sacrifice of them in it. He catches too a shift of pronoun across the two verses, from children borne to God to children simply his, the offence aggravated by giving the idol what belonged to him; and he renders the closing question as asking whether the harlotry was too little, apostasy alone not being enough without this crime. Wesley distinguishes consecrating children as priests to dumb idols from burning them outright; Gill notes that the children were not the parents own only but the Lord.

Calvin treats the act as the extinction of something natural. Philosophers place among the principles of nature the affection a parent bears a child, and when that ceases a man becomes a monster; yet these supposed that in killing their offspring they obeyed God. Against that he sets the one case that might seem to justify it. Abraham prepared to offer his son, but had a clear command, and his obedience rested on faith; these had no command at all, and are condemned for prodigious madness.

On what passing through the fire meant, Clarke and Calvin reach for the same classical passage, quoted by Clarke from Bishop Newcome, in which fires are made before the tents and the people brought out to leap over the flames for the purging of their pollutions. Clarke infers that the phrase does not always mean the child was consumed, but served as a rite of consecration. Calvin uses it to establish two kinds of offering, the children not always being slain; here, he says, the prophet speaks of the crueller kind.

Calvin then explains in what sense the children could be called the children of God, by distinguishing two elections. Speaking generally, God chose the whole family of Abraham, circumcision being the seal of adoption; but there was another election, secret, by which he took out of that multitude whom he pleased, and these are the sons of promise. The people spoken of here were unbelievers, strangers in whom the secret election did not flourish, yet his people in respect of external profession. To the objection that the outward sign was therefore useless, he answers that God honoured those miserable men by opening a way to the hope of life through the outward testimonies of adoption. Gill reaches the same phrase by a shorter road, calling them his by creation and by national adoption.

Calvin makes forgetfulness the root of it. Had the slavery they were delivered from been present to their minds they would not have been so blinded; he asks how unfaithful wives come to despise their husbands except by being dazzled with their own beauty. On the verse that opens the next section he records a reading he rejects. Some take the first clause separately as a threat that their condition would revert, the nakedness laid bare again, as another prophet threatens; Calvin calls that forced and joins the clause to what follows, treating the doubled cry of woe as an exclamation abruptly interposed. To the objection that building high places was no worse than their other sins he answers that God speaks not of one altar but of every sign of idolatry with which they had infected the land, each a testimony of backsliding and the whole an open boast that they meant to overthrow what he had prescribed. Ellicott marks the same verse as a turn, since the idolatry described so far was taken chiefly from the old inhabitants of the land, while what follows was eagerly adopted from foreign nations. Keil and Delitzsch render the new buildings arches rather than an eminent place, and the penalty a diminished allowance, adding that even the neighbours who hated her were ashamed of her way.
24:
Gill takes the eminent place for a brothel, the Septuagint reading it a whoring house and the Targum an altar, while the word itself carries the signification of a pit or ditch; what had been done privately was now housed in public. Clarke runs the word through its versions, one giving a stew, his old manuscript Bible a bordel house, and Coverdale rendering it that thou hast builded thy stewes and bordell houses in every place; Diodati has thou hast built a brothel. Bordel he calls an Italian word, of which he is sure the modern brothel is a corruption. Ellicott renders the word literally arches, arched rooms being used in idol worship for licentious ends. Wesley says only that idol temples stood in every street, in Jerusalem and in her cities.

Calvin uses this section to press a claim he says the interpreters miss. They think the prophet is always discoursing of idols and superstitions, but weighing the circumstances he finds two different charges: that the Jews vitiated the worship of God by their own fictions, and that they flew now to Egypt, now to Assyria, and so entangled themselves in forbidden treaties. It is a common method with the prophets to call such covenants fornication, since a wife ought to lie under the shadow of her husband, and God wished the people content under his protection.

Ellicott explains why Egypt is named first: even at the golden calf the people turned with avidity to the worship of Egypt. He accounts for the phrase great of flesh from the thoroughly sensuous nature worship of that people, and observes that the connection was political as well as religious, in bold defiance of repeated commands, so that much of the work of Jeremiah was to oppose the leaning of the kings of Judah toward that alliance. Gill says the same of the leagues. Wesley reads great of flesh simply of men of great stature.

Clarke glosses the diminished ordinary as the household provision made for a wife, her food and clothing. Calvin arrives independently at the same sense, setting aside the rendering of Jerome, who took the word for a statute and explained it of the law, and asking how that agrees with the simile of the husband kept up throughout. He counts two chastisements here, the taking away of what had been assigned for food and ornament, and the delivering up to enemies; and he opens the whole with the proverb that fools grow wise only by the rod. Ellicott draws the sting of the shame of the Philistines differently: true to their own false gods, they despised Israel for unfaithfulness, which he calls the old but ever new story of the heathen repelled from the truth by the unworthiness of its professed followers.

On the Assyrian verse Calvin again refuses the idolatry reading, since the prophets were not accustomed to say that a people committed fornication with the Assyrians because they imitated their worship; the charge is the sending for aid when Israel and Syria pressed, which was like thrusting God from his place. Gill points to Ahaz, who sent to Tiglathpileser and copied the altar he saw. Ellicott notes how strange the double alliance was, Assyria and Egypt being for centuries in deadly hostility, and yet the altar in the temple court displaced for one of the gods of Assyria. On the last verse he prefers the sense of traffic for Canaan, the word applied elsewhere to Babylon, so that the idolatries begun in the land were carried outward along her commerce until they reached Chaldea. Calvin canvasses the readings that make Canaan the old inhabitants, or a country next to Chaldea, and calls them forced, taking the particle for one of likeness: a woman meeting a stranger sins with less disgrace than one who runs abroad to seek followers.
30:
Calvin opens by noting that the prophet seems at variance with himself, comparing the people to a strong and imperious woman and in the same breath calling their heart dissolute. He answers that in despisers of God both faults are to be blamed at once: they flow away like water and yet are hard as rocks. The heart here stands for the seat of the intellect. Ellicott says the ordinary word for weak scarcely carries the force of the original, which is languishing with desire, and observes that the word for heart stands here only in the feminine. Wesley has her unstable like water and imperious as a woman who knows no superior and will be neither guided nor governed.

On the high places Calvin keeps the figure rather than the altar, reading them as tents pitched conspicuously to attract followers from a distance, and draws a lesson from the severity of the rebuke. Who, he asks, would think it so great a crime to build an altar on a high place to the honour of God? Yet the prophet abhors it; the worship of God is not to be estimated by our own perception, and since obedience is the principal part of that worship and is preferred to all sacrifices, what we might tolerate ought to be detested. Ellicott turns the verse outward: after the division it was characteristic of both kingdoms to seek foreign interference first and to purchase it at a heavy price. Set on the great highway between Egypt and Assyria, their friendship ought to have been worth courting; instead they threw themselves away and bought their own ruin.

The inversion of the figure occupies them all. Wesley states it plainly: common harlots live by the gain of their looseness, while this one lavishes out credit and wealth to maintain her adulterers. Gill notes that she was provided with food and clothing and had no cause to prostitute herself for a livelihood; he adds the distinction that in a people married to the Lord idolatry was adultery, while the same sin among the Gentiles was simple fornication. Calvin canvasses the reading that makes her an adulteress under her own roof, who never divorces her husband but stays at home to admit strangers; he prefers the simpler sense of one who admits strangers in her husband stead, induced not by want but by her own lust. On the gifts he presses the extravagance: they spared no expense in attracting lovers, and he likens it to the man who grudges a farthing for the relief of the poor and throws away guineas to compound for his sins. Calvin makes them worse than harlots on that ground, since the hope of gain is at least a pretext and a starving woman may be driven to excess, but far fouler is she who purchases her lovers; Wesley reads the same verse as showing what the nature of men is when God leaves them to themselves.

Ellicott marks the structural break here, the sin described to this point and the punishment now pronounced, first in terms drawn from the legal punishment of the adulteress and murderess and then in a vindication of the justice of the doom by comparison with Samaria on one side and Sodom on the other; he refers the gifts to the silver and gold Ahaz took from the house of the Lord to secure the alliance of the king of Assyria. Henry takes up the sentence as a court scene, adultery being by the law of Moses a capital crime and the prisoner already found guilty. When God speaks in wrath, he says, he will be justified and clear when he judges, the sins of the condemned so set in order before them that their mouth is stopped and they have not a word to object against the equity of the sentence.
36:
The opening word divides the commentators. Gill reports that the Rabbins use it for the bottom of a thing, and that Kimchi and Ben Melech take it of a woman lower part, while Jarchi makes it a flux poured out on her lovers. Clarke observes that the word names a metal and is generally supposed to mean money, but adds that it also means verdigris, the poisonous rust of copper or brass, and asks whether it does not point to a disease bred by promiscuous connexions. Ellicott settles on money without hesitation: gold or silver is the commoner term, so the prophet has used brass contemptuously.

Ellicott then lays out the legal ground. Death was the penalty for adultery, and the same for devoting seed to an idol and for murder; the customary execution of an individual was by stoning and of an apostate city by the sword, which is why both modes appear together here, though he grants it is somewhat at the expense of the consistency of the allegory. He would render the closing clause that God will make her blood of fury and jealousy, the fury answering to the avenging of murder and the jealousy to the punishment of adultery. Calvin turns the same doubleness against the plea of good intention. They thought they obeyed; but nothing is more disgraceful than under the pretense of piety to slay and burn ones own children, and when they pleaded their zeal God branded wickedness upon them. Wesley puts the exchange in one line: they gave the blood of their children to idols, and their own will be given them to drink.

Ellicott notes that the hereditary foes shared the spoil as well as the allies, naming the Philistines and the Edomites. Calvin recalls that by the time Jerusalem fell the Assyrians had been reduced under the Chaldeans, so the strength of both was joined against her. Clarke reads the stripping as the ordinary end of such a life, the maintainers taking back in the end all they had given. On the altars Calvin sets aside the rendering house of sin, holding that the prophet names the altars themselves; and on the stones he doubts the suggestion that engines of war are meant.

Calvin explains why burning is added to killing. When men are slain others may succeed them if they find houses standing and fields tilled, but when all is consumed by fire hope for the future is taken away. He adds that the ridicule was harder to bear than the perishing, and cites the psalm that remembers the sons of Edom crying down with it in the day of Jerusalem.

The last crux is what it means for the fury to rest. Gill offers both readings, that God contends no longer once a reformation is brought about, or that the wrath abides until an utter end is made. Ellicott is blunt that it is not in pity but in satiety. Calvin agrees that no mitigation is promised, the consumption being itself the rest of the indignation; he allows the reading of the second word as jealousy, since a husband avenging an injury is inflamed with it, but once he begins to think his wife unworthy of further notice the indignation is allayed. Wesley says the same of an abused husband whose anger ceases in the public punishment of the adulteress. Clarke reads the quiet as complete abandonment, and when God in judgment ceases to reprehend, that is the severest judgment of all. Ellicott corrects fretted to raged against, and prefers the first person against the Masoretic pointing, so that God says it would be wrong to let such sin go unpunished. Clarke traces the whole collapse to forgetfulness, ingratitude being the commencement if not the parent of many crimes; and Calvin adds that they thought God less munificent than he ought to be.
44:
Henry opens with the habit the section is aimed at. We are all apt to judge of ourselves by comparison, and to imagine we are good enough if we are but as good as some who pass; so the prophet sets Jerusalem beside the places that went before her and shows her worse than any. The mother is the nations that possessed the land first, and the daughter is like her in temper as if she had been her own child: the mother loathed her husband and her children. They had been warned not to do after the abominations of the men of that land, but they learned their way and trod in their steps, so that in respect of imitation it could truly be said their mother was a Hittite and their father an Amorite.

Calvin explains why the saying is quoted at all. A man who surpasses all others in cruelty and lust becomes notorious and is pointed at in vulgar sayings; the charge is that they had supplied material for every buffoon and wit to laugh at their expense. He then asks why the proverb holds. Daughters do often degenerate from the best mothers; but the usual case is a wicked mother with daughters like herself, and this happens less by nature than by education, since a woman of perverse inclination thinks a stigma attaches to her if her daughter is better, and so forms her after her own morals. Few daughters are modest whose mothers are immodest, few sober who were brought up by drunkards. Clarke reaches the same conclusion through common sayings, as is the breeding so is the practice, and draws from them the necessity of early holy precepts supported by suitable example. Gill takes the proverb makers for men with a talent at satirizing and scoffing, such as Lucian and others.

Ellicott raises a difficulty about the sisters. If Samaria and Sodom loathed their husbands, in what sense had they husbands to loathe? He answers that they are still regarded as having gone astray from a primeval revelation and proved false to the only true God whom they once had known. On elder and younger he insists the words mean greater and smaller, coming like the Latin major and minor to serve for age, but keeping their first sense here, since Sodom was not chronologically younger than Jerusalem. The left and right he explains by the Orientals describing position as though facing the east, which puts Samaria on the left and Sodom on the right. Clarke, however, doubts the identification, supposing that Sodom here means those who dwelt beyond Jordan in the land of the Moabites and Ammonites, since the city existed before Jerusalem had a name. Gill grounds the elder sister on descent, one father between them, the northern kingdom greater in number and power and first in the apostasy.

On the excess Ellicott would render the clause that she had not walked after their ways a little only, but had done more corruptly, and he measures the aggravation by time: Sodom had sinned grievously in its day, but a thousand years and more had passed since, and Samaria had gone into captivity a century before the prophet. Calvin finds a method in the order of the charges. Had the prophet said at the first word that they were worse than the men of Sodom they would have listened less; by first proposing the incredible thing, and only then pronouncing that they had surpassed mother and sisters both, he stirred their minds more vehemently. The denial that they walked in those ways he restricts to the sense of equality, not exemption, their impiety being the more detestable; they did not walk in their ways only because they had left them far behind. Wesley says it in a line, that all things considered those others were the lesser sinners.
48:
The oath draws comment for what it had to carry. Gill notes that God, having no greater to swear by, swore by himself and his life. Calvin makes the difficulty sharper. Even now, he says, no one will suffer a city or a nation to be compared with Sodom; anyone using the phrase inflames all against himself. They had a further ground of indignation, since God had marked them with magnificent titles, a nation of priests, his inheritance, his son and his firstborn. That is why the oath was necessary.

On the iniquity of Sodom all four are struck by the list. Ellicott observes that the description strikes at causes rather than overt acts, and that the crimes always associated with that name are not mentioned, while the sin specified is the negative one too common in every age, that she did not strengthen the hand of the poor and needy. Clarke draws the same conclusion: the city was guilty of much besides the offence for which she is remembered, and pride, luxury, idleness and uncharitableness were enough to sink any city. Wesley calls the first item the fountain and occasion of all, glosses fulness of bread as excess in eating and drinking, and the last clause a refusal to help strangers.

Calvin uses the same list to anatomise pride, the mother of all contempt of God and of all cruelty, so that we cannot be restrained unless moderation and humility reign within us. Pride, he says, has two horns. One is when men forget their own condition and claim what God alone calls his own; the other is when they will not acknowledge their vices and please themselves in enormities as though no account were ever to be rendered. Ellicott corrects the next clause, the word rendered good having no equivalent in the original and the particle meaning when, so that the sense is that he took them away when he saw this.

The comparison with Samaria is harder. Sound worship continued at Jerusalem while the northern tribes openly abandoned the law; how then can the Jews be called worse? Ingratitude has great influence in exaggerating a crime, and God had kept this small band as the very flower of the people when the ten tribes were all but absorbed; and further, they had watched how severely he avenged the superstitions of that kingdom, and were so far from repenting that they courted its alliance. Gill reaches the same verdict by counting advantages: the temple among them, the priests to officiate, the prophets to teach, and the captivity of the ten tribes which they refused as warning.

On the word justified they agree and then diverge. Ellicott says it is plainly comparative, the greatness of the sin making even the sisters appear innocent beside her; Wesley that they were not made righteous but declared less unrighteous. Clarke renders it that they shall be justified more than thou, and finds the phrase casting light on the man who went down to his house justified rather than the other, less blame attaching to one who had fewer advantages and was truly penitent while the other boasted. Calvin sees an inconsistency between justifying the sisters and judging them, and resolves it by separating the senses. They justified them not by any sentence of absolution but by making themselves worthy of double condemnation; the judging means that they insulted over their brethren when the kingdom fell, which he calls the common way of hypocrites, to grow hot against others as if that covered their own crimes. Ellicott closes on what follows: restoration is first declared impossible, and the attempts of many commentators to turn that language into a covert promise are entirely unsuccessful; only afterwards is the covenant promised. He finds no contradiction, since the doom is pronounced on the nation as a whole and the exception is then made for the few.
53:
Everything here turns on whether the promised turn of captivity is a promise at all. Ellicott is emphatic that it is not, and states the hopelessness of the punishment in the strongest possible form. The phrase need not mean a return from exile, since Sodom was never carried into one, but a return to the former estate; and that was manifestly impossible for Sodom, whose daughters had perished ages before, leaving no descendants, while for Samaria it would lack historical identification. Calvin argues the same way, that the prophet reasons from an impossibility, as if he had said, you shall be safe when Sodom and Samaria are, and compares the manner of speaking to a line of Virgil naming a thing that can never happen. He notes that some corrupt the passage into a promise by taking the Sodomites to mean the Moabites and Ammonites, the descendants of Lot, and answers that a child may see this is trifling. Wesley reaches the same conclusion from history: though God brought some of the two tribes out of Babylon they were never again so rich or renowned. Then, he adds, and not before.

Calvin meets the objection that return home is promised elsewhere, and answers with a distinction. The prophets speak of the people in two ways. Sometimes they regard the whole body of the nation in the mass, and since that body had excluded itself from mercy, no hope of mercy remained; but afterwards they change their discourse to the remnant, for God always preserves a hidden seed so that the church is not utterly extinguished, though it is sometimes preserved miserably as in a sepulchre. Gill records the older opinion that in the days of an expected deliverer the city would be restored, as the garden of God and as the land of Egypt, and the reading of Jarchi that the land of brimstone and salt would be healed and inhabited; but he refuses the literal sense, reading it of the calling and conversion of the nations.

The comfort the sisters receive is read as a bitter one. Ellicott makes it the counterpart of the justifying already spoken of, the greater sin throwing their own evil into the shade. Calvin says God is speaking after the ordinary manner of men, since the miserable feel some consolation in seeing themselves perish among a great multitude. Wesley makes it encouragement given to sinners like those cities.

On the silence about Sodom, Calvin points to what they had before their eyes and what ought to have kept them in fear: a region once like the paradise of God, as Moses calls it, and in the middle of that fertility a lake of sulphur and bitumen, material enough for instruction unless they were utterly sluggish. Those who shut their eyes to manifest judgments he compares to the brutes; and he traces the fault to prosperity, since while things went to their wish they were not anxious about rendering an account. Gill offers two accounts of the silence, either that the destruction was not talked of, not reported from father to son, or that the name was so infamous that they scorned to mention it.

Gill draws the sharpest line: it is a sad thing to know sin only by having it discovered in the punishment of it. Ellicott corrects the pronoun, reading simply the reproach, and dates the pride to the days of prosperity: the pride was humbled by the disasters that fell from the days of Ahaz onward, when she was hard pressed by the Syrians and the Philistines and impoverished herself to buy aid from Assyria. He mentions but doubts another view, which refers the reproach to her own exultation at the fall of Syria and the Philistines before the march of the Assyrians. Wesley reads the same verse of the nations round about combined in league against the house of David.
58:
Calvin reads the first verse as closing off complaint. Against a people bold in expostulation he pronounces that what they bear is not any immoderate rigour but their own wickedness; and if they weighed their enormities these would be found heavier than his treatment of them. Gill says their sin was to be read in their punishment, and Wesley glosses the word as its punishment.

The charge of breaking the covenant raises the question whether God is then free. Calvin sets the objection: whatever they were, God had bound himself, having adopted Abraham with his seed, and so ought to stand to his agreement. He answers that covenanting requires mutual faith, that a man deceived is no longer bound to a perfidious breaker of agreements, and that there is no covenant when either party declines it; their perfidy had given God the liberty of rejecting them. Ellicott makes the breach the especial heinousness of the sin, since guilt is proportioned to the light against which it is committed. Wesley states it in one clause, that as they broke the covenant so will he break his.

Henry takes the close as the point of the chapter. After a shameful conviction and a dreadful denunciation, mercy is remembered and mercy is reserved for those who come after. He allows that the earlier words about the return of the two sisters may be read as a promise if the name is taken of the Moabites and Ammonites, the posterity of Lot, but is sure that these closing verses are one, in part fulfilled at the return of the reformed people out of Babylon. It is to our comfort and advantage, he says, that God deals with us in a covenant way, since the mercies of a covenant come to be sure mercies and everlasting.

When the days of youth were is disputed. Gill dates the covenant remembered to Sinai, and cites Kimchi that the time from Egypt until they came into the land was called the days of their youth. Clarke dates it instead to Abraham, in whom they began to be a nation. Wesley holds both together, the covenant made in the loins of Abraham and solemnly renewed after the coming out of Egypt. Calvin holds that the prophet now restrains himself and speaks peculiarly to the election of grace: the promise is not common to all the sons of Abraham according to the flesh but peculiar to a small band reserved. God recalls the faithful to the fountain, he says, lest they claim anything as their right; the pity has no foundation but the covenant itself.

Whether the covenant promised is new or the old renewed divides them. Calvin says that a better and more excellent one is promised than the ancient covenant already abolished through the fault of the people. Ellicott holds that the later covenant was both the continuation and the designed fulfilment of the earlier, and points to the contrast between the covenant God calls his own here and the one he calls theirs in the next verse. On the sisters, Ellicott says the humiliation must be so complete that she will gladly receive these once despised enemies into the closest family relation, and that we are not to think of one city but of what it represented, the heathen world at large. Clarke names the elder and younger as the nations called before and after, and Wesley as those admitted into communion, not by the ceremonies but by the covenant that writes the law in the heart. Gill makes the shame the effect of covenant grace applied, bringing a man to blush at what he has been guilty of; Calvin makes it the condition, since grace is offered to all in common but none receive it except those who condemn themselves, and if we wish our sins to be buried before God we must remember them ourselves.
62:
The commentators divide over how much continuity to allow between the old covenant and the new. Ellicott states it as a merging: the old, having failed, is taken up into the new and better one, which is established through a perfect Mediator, though the way for it had to be prepared by the less perfect covenant of old. Calvin puts the relation the other way round, insisting that the covenant made with Abraham could not be abolished by the perfidy of man, and citing the rule that even if the whole world were liars God must always remain true. The covenant is new, he grants, and yet it has its origin from the old, so that those reconciled are grafted into the body of the ancient church and made sons of Abraham. It is established, then, not with the people already deserted through its perfidy, but with the true and genuine children of Abraham.

Calvin draws a further consequence from that. The covenant could not be constituted afresh unless a new people were formed and God created a new world; he takes the psalm that says a people shall be created to praise God as the pattern of it, and hears in the phrase an oblique reproof, as though the praises of God had been abolished among them. He is careful to keep the promise limited, since the safety of the whole nation was already desperate and this discourse belongs specially to the elect. Gill notes that the establishing is repeated for the comfort of a people ashamed at their own ways, and to show its certainty.

On the last verse Ellicott makes a lexical correction: rather than pacified toward thee, the sense is when I pardon thee, the original being the word used technically in the law for the atonement or covering up of sins, so that the thought is of God forgiving his people. Gill reads the effect: the more a man knows of God as his covenant God the more he remembers his former ways and reflects on them with shame.

Calvin uses the verse to hold together two things that cannot be divided, the testimony of grace and the doctrine of repentance, calling their union the substance of the gospel, that God wishes those to repent whom he reconciles by gratuitous pardon. What is commended here, he adds, is not only penitence but the continual desire of it. It is troublesome to be often shaking off our sins, so we escape from the perception of them and every one willingly puts his own out of sight; for if we do look at them they compel us to be ashamed and then wound us with serious grief, conscience summoning us to a tribunal where the vengeance would slay even the boldest were they not upheld by the assurance of pardon. Since the acknowledgment of sins brings both shame and sorrow, we try to put it away; and yet no other access to the favour of God is open to us.

Wesley reads the closing clause as forbidding three things, that she is neither to justify herself, nor to condemn others, nor to quarrel with her God. He then turns it into a proportion: the more we feel of the love of God the more ashamed we are that we ever offended him, and the more our shame for sin is increased the more our comfort in God will be increased also. Clarke ends by standing back from the chapter. He directs the reader to his note on the thirteenth verse as the key to its principal metaphors, warning that anyone who disregards it will do justice neither to himself nor the prophet, and sums up the chapter as a tissue of invective, sharp, cutting and confounding, everywhere well sustained, in every respect richly merited, and in no case leaving the delinquent any room for justification or response.
